stories.summary: When George Everest chose a place to live, he picked a stunning spot in Mussoorie overlooking a forested valley where, Ajay recalls, tigers once roamed. Over the years Everest House became a run-down white marble building, caught in legal disputes but open to anyone who wandered in. Ajay loved sitting there and imagining Everest's life after mapping the country. On his last visit, government agencies were doing ugly, tasteless construction to turn it into a museum.
stories.insight: Some places carry history best when left alone. Restoring heritage takes taste as well as money, and an official makeover can destroy the very atmosphere that made a place worth visiting.
stories.quote: You could feel what it was like to be George Everest, to have built the first map of this country, and then to be living in that bungalow on the edge of that valley and the forest.

stories.topic: The Maps India Wouldn't Sell Its Own People
stories.summary: When Ajay grew old enough to want serious maps, he found that the Survey of India's sheets were often decades out of date (some regions last surveyed around 1934). They came only at a coarse 1:200,000 scale, not the 1:10,000 or 1:20,000 a hiker needs. Worse, maps within about 100 km of the border, including the whole coastline, could not be sold, on the grounds that terrorists might use them. Living in Bombay, he was cut off from coastal maps, and hiking in the Himalayas he was cut off from border maps. The same maps sit in a museum in London.
stories.insight: Security rules can take a public good away from the citizens who paid for it while barely slowing down a real adversary. The cost of the rule falls on the people, and the threat is untouched.
stories.quote: Like you're taking my tax money, you're making these maps, but then you're saying, No, we will refuse to sell these maps in India for security considerations.

stories.topic: Barun Mitra, Tribal Land Rights and Google Earth
stories.summary: Barun Mitra and fellow activists were fighting for the land rights of tribals, in Gujarat as Amit remembers it. The tribals had no proof that they had occupied the land long enough to qualify. The activists used historical Google Earth satellite images to go back in time and presented them as evidence in court, and the tribals won. Ajay adds that this was before Android phones, so the team walked the ground with Garmin handheld GPS units and fed the coordinates into Google Earth. Afterwards the tribals, who had lived there for years without building anything pakka or adding toilets, began building toilets.
stories.insight: Secure property rights change incentives. People invest in the land under them once they know it is theirs, and satellite imagery from a private company became the evidence that made those rights possible.
stories.quote: But the moment they had the land right, the incentive changed, and they built toilets.

stories.topic: His Father's Wall-Sized Map of India
stories.summary: In Ajay's childhood home there was a map twice his height. His father had taken the four Survey of India sheets that together made up the country, pasted them onto a wooden board and fixed it to the wall. Young Ajay stared at it constantly, learning rivers, memorising district and place names, and working out the best routes between places. As an adult he has never found a modern wall map of India of National Geographic or Rand McNally quality, and he asks listeners to point him to one.
stories.insight: A small act by a parent can start a lifelong passion. And even now, something as simple as a good wall map of India is hard to buy.
stories.quote: I just constantly would look at that and try to get a sense of the land and understand each river and try to mug up the names of every district and every place name and think of what is an optimal route from here to there. It was a treat.

stories.topic: A Generation That Will Never Be Lost
stories.summary: Amit recalls a friend's remark that stopped him in his tracks. Because of GPS and phone maps, people born today will never know what it feels like to be lost. Amit adds that this is also a loss of a kind, but leaves it there.
stories.insight: Technologies quietly remove whole experiences from human life. Something every earlier generation knew can vanish within one generation without anyone noticing.
stories.quote: He said that people in the generation who are born today will never know what it is to be lost.

stories.topic: How Google Decided to Map the Whole World from Hyderabad
stories.summary: Google first assumed that where governments, as in the US and UK, released map data, the job was done. That approach failed in countries like India, where the government either doesn't have the data or won't release it. Ajay credits Sanjay Jain as a pioneer who pushed Google to raise its ambition. Jain and others wrote software called MapMaker, and a large facility in Hyderabad, which Ajay estimates at 5,000 to 10,000 people, now traces roads, bridges, buildings and rivers from satellite imagery to build Google's map of the entire world.
stories.insight: When the state fails to provide a public good, a private firm with enough ambition can build it, and in this case the work is done from India itself.
stories.quote: So they upped their game saying, No, we will make the map for the whole world.

stories.topic: Apple, iPods and How MP3 Won
stories.summary: In the early iPod and iTunes era, Ajay says, Apple sold music in a proprietary format that only worked on Apple devices, even though you had paid for the file. The rest of the industry saw the threat of an Apple monopoly over the world's music and agreed to build rival systems on MP3, an open format anyone can read and write. Consumers got angry and Apple backed off. Ajay sees the same pattern in maps: Microsoft, Amazon and others, alarmed by Google's lead, now use OpenStreetMap and feed it corporate data, including GPS traces from Amazon deliveries.
stories.insight: Dominance creates its own opposition. When one firm gets too powerful, its rivals have a reason to cooperate on open standards, which ends up benefiting everyone.
stories.quote: Like you would pay money to buy music from the Apple music store, but the file sitting on your disc was not yours because you couldn't decrypt it.

stories.topic: Going From Tall to Short Without Shrinking
stories.summary: At college Ajay was tall for his generation. Today he is short compared with 20- and 25-year-olds. His height hasn't changed; the people around him have grown taller as India has developed.
stories.insight: Economic development shows up in people's bodies. One person's position in the height distribution can track a country's progress over a lifetime.
stories.quote: So that's the economic development and the improvements of India within my life. That I've gone from being a reasonably tall person to being a reasonably short person.

stories.topic: Taller in First Class, Shorter in Second
stories.summary: When Amit first came to Bombay in the mid-1990s, he noticed something on the local trains that disturbed him: people in first class were generally taller than people in second class. He admits this is anecdotal and not backed by data. Separately, he notes that a cousin of almost the same age who grew up in the US turned out much stronger than him. He also wonders whether, among four brothers, the youngest ends up tallest because the family has prospered by the time he grows up.
stories.insight: Inequality can literally be seen in people's height, shaped by childhood nutrition and illness, not just in their incomes.
stories.quote: the people in first class were taller than the people in second class.

recommendations.creator: Robert Bly
recommendations.context: Amit reads this short poem aloud to open the episode.
recommendations.reason: It is a great poem, and it shows how a whole universe can fit into something small, which sets up an episode about maps.

recommendations.creator: Magnetic Fields
recommendations.context: A song by Stephen Merritt that Amit had just discovered. He reads its lyrics about a book 'full of charts and facts and figures and instructions for dancing.'
recommendations.reason: Its idea of something old and mysterious leads into how mysterious the world once was before maps. Ajay adds that love is still a mystery, but our understanding of space has been transformed.

recommendations.creator: John Keay
recommendations.reason: It tells the story of the early Survey of India and the first mapping of the country. In his words, it is 'a heroic tale' and 'so much fun.'

recommendations.creator: Ridley Scott
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation of the day: an early-nineties road movie, chosen because it is about travelling rather than maps.
recommendations.reason: It is one of his favourite films of all time. It comes with a story he says 'should be true' even if it isn't: Saudi censors cut every shot of women driving, leaving a four-minute film.

recommendations.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
recommendations.context: Amit reads the full one-paragraph story aloud while discussing Google Maps.
recommendations.reason: It is a short parable about cartographers who make a map as large as the empire itself, and it shows the limits of any static map. A perfectly accurate map would be as big as the world and out of date the next moment.

recommendations.creator: Free To Choose Network (presented by Johan Norberg)
recommendations.context: A documentary Amit cites for the story of Barun Mitra using historical Google Earth images to win land rights for tribals.
recommendations.reason: It covers an inspiring real case in which satellite data, used as court evidence, secured property rights and changed incentives on the ground.

recommendations.creator: Google
recommendations.context: The first of three systems Ajay says have given Indians a 'map paradise.'
recommendations.reason: He calls it 'a madly great map.' It is free to users and routes you on foot, by car or by public transport through any city. Ajay himself regularly contributes corrections and missing places.

recommendations.creator: Google
recommendations.context: Ajay urges listeners to install the desktop version rather than only using the web version.
recommendations.reason: On a big screen in terrain mode, its 3D views and aerial flybys are 'a delight' and 'paradise.' He thinks people should be willing to pay a lot for it, though it is currently free.

recommendations.context: The third system Ajay describes: an open map database built by volunteers worldwide.
recommendations.reason: It is the true digital public good: public domain, free to download, non-rival and non-excludable, and anyone can contribute. Indian volunteers hold OSM mapping parties.

recommendations.item: Did the Indian GDP just jump up by a basis point?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls writing this blog post when Google launched Google Maps navigation in India.
recommendations.reason: It makes the case that free navigation creates a huge consumer surplus for every user, large enough to ask whether it showed up in GDP.

core_ideas.concept: Maps Take You From Darkness to Light
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay asks you to picture Akbar or Aurangzeb ruling a country they couldn't see. Without maps, rulers had only local knowledge held in local languages and passed along through Chinese whispers. Locals might want a payment for information or mislead travellers on purpose. You could solve local problems but never see the whole picture, plan routes, assess revenue or decide where to build. A good map makes local guides unnecessary: anyone, from anywhere, can see the land and make plans.
core_ideas.quote: So you don't need to be a local it is a way of banging away at the nativism that otherwise every region suffers from.

core_ideas.explanation: A printed map is only one way of showing the underlying data, which is a list of coordinates with properties attached. Thinking of maps as data explains how one survey can produce topo sheets, road maps and national maps. It also explains why releasing the database matters more than printing sheets.
core_ideas.quote: So at heart, maps is data. It's a list of coordinates which have certain properties.

core_ideas.concept: Maps as a Public Good That Belongs to the People
core_ideas.explanation: Surveying a country is enormously costly, but once it is done, each extra copy of a map costs almost nothing. Maps are non-rival (my use doesn't reduce yours) and non-excludable, which makes them a classic public good and one of the British administration's early achievements in India. Ajay argues that a public good the state keeps to itself is worthless. Rich countries release such data freely, for example the US TIGER database, which anyone can download without registering. Indian agencies like ISRO and the Survey of India keep theirs locked away.
core_ideas.quote: Remember, a public good is for the people. It's not there for the state. We don't give a damn about what the state has in their pocket.

core_ideas.concept: Every Map Is a Model of the World
core_ideas.explanation: No single map does everything. Topo sheets, transport maps and political maps each simplify reality for a particular purpose. Google Maps is superb for navigation but won't show district boundaries, so if your unit of interest is a district, it's the wrong model. Choose the map that suits the question you are asking.
core_ideas.quote: So again, every map is a model of the world that is useful for certain things, and then you want different models of the world that are useful for different things.

core_ideas.concept: Driving by the Headlights: Mundane Work Adds Up
core_ideas.explanation: Amit sees George Everest as both dreamer and doer. The individual surveyor noting hill heights never saw the big picture and might not live to see the finished map; he did his small task as his dharma. Amit borrows the novelist E.L. Doctorow's image: you can drive the whole distance seeing only as far as your headlights. Ajay adds that gathering data and building statistics take decades of patient work without immediate reward, and the effort eventually adds up to something spectacular.
core_ideas.quote: And I find this also a great metaphor, that you know, the way that a map is made, that's the way a person is made.

core_ideas.concept: The Technologies That Replaced the Theodolite
core_ideas.explanation: Accurate maps once required thousands of people walking the country with theodolites, which only a state as capable as British India could manage. Four technologies changed this. GPS gives roughly 10-metre precision using US Department of Defense satellites that only broadcast while the handset works out its own position. Satellite photographs can be traced over like translucent paper. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) reveals buildings in 3D, and digital elevation maps capture terrain. On top of these come GPS traces from millions of Android phones, which reveal where roads exist and how fast traffic moves on them. Ajay also urges listeners to switch off location tracking on their phones.
core_ideas.quote: All they do is shout. They only broadcast. That's all. And they don't know the existence of a handset.

core_ideas.concept: An End Run Around Low State Capacity
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay sees India's failures as a general pattern of underdevelopment rather than the fault of any one agency: monetary policy, police, courts, the military and the Survey of India all work badly. Reforming the Survey of India would take a generation of visionary leaders. Instead, Google Maps, Google Earth and OpenStreetMap, all built on public goods paid for by rich-country taxpayers, have given Indians better maps than George Everest ever had, without using Indian tax money or Indian state capacity.
core_ideas.quote: It's like an end run around the entire state capacity problem of getting the survey of India to work.

core_ideas.concept: Borges's Map and the Live Map
core_ideas.explanation: Borges's parable of a map as big as the empire shows that a perfectly accurate map would be as large as the world and out of date the moment it was finished. Amit's point is that Google Maps gets around this by updating continuously, rerouting you as traffic changes. Even with every resource he could want, George Everest could only have produced a static map.
core_ideas.quote: a truly accurate map of the world would have to be as big as the world. And As a corollary to that, in the very next moment, it would be outdated because the world is constantly in flux and changing.

core_ideas.concept: OSM: What a Digital Public Good Really Means
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay complains that the phrase 'digital public good' is widely misused. A true one is non-rival and non-excludable, like the Linux source code or OpenStreetMap data. OSM began with map databases released by rich countries, then grew through volunteers who map their own neighbourhoods, and is now strengthened by corporations wary of Google. No coercion or taxation was involved; it is the energy of the people.
core_ideas.quote: The OSM data is public domain. It is sitting on websites. It is available for download. It is non-rival, it is non-excludable, it is the digital public good.

core_ideas.concept: When One Firm Gets Too Powerful, Rivals Cooperate
core_ideas.explanation: Monopoly threats produce counter-coalitions. The music industry backed the open MP3 format against Apple's lock-in, and Microsoft, Amazon and others now back OSM against Google. As a side benefit, sophisticated corporate users improve open systems through complaints, bug reports and feature demands.
core_ideas.quote: That if one firm becomes too powerful, the others get an incentive to cooperate.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that the Indian state's first reaction to citizens making their own maps has been to ban them: restricting private mapping, resisting Google Street View, and blocking purchases of foreign satellite imagery. As with neglecting coal deaths while fixating on terrorism, invoking security can justify banning almost anything. Technology alone isn't enough; it has to be paired with a liberal pushback against the coercive state.
core_ideas.quote: Instead of solving the problem of coal, the government will say terrorism. And then suddenly, you know, you can ban anything under the excuse of terrorism.

core_ideas.concept: Technology as the Source of Liberal Hope
core_ideas.explanation: Amit takes a cautionary point from the story: we tend to assume the world is fixed, that only the state can provide certain things and that the state is moribund. He says he is full of despair about the world, but technology gives him hope because it empowers individuals in ways political movements have not. Even the smartphone, despite being a surveillance and distraction machine, is full of tools that give people freedom.
core_ideas.quote: technology can empower individuals in a way that political movements have failed to do.

core_ideas.concept: Lines on a Map Are Temporary
core_ideas.explanation: Amit sees a 'crumbling of the mainstream' across media and entertainment, and wonders whether nation-states might be next. Political borders are man-made and history shows they don't last. Maps of languages, dialects or cuisines can be just as revealing, and on the ground the borders simply aren't visible. Ajay has walked to the edge of the India-China border in Ladakh and Uttarakhand and found only the Himalaya.
core_ideas.quote: All of those lines are temporary. They are man made and they're temporary, that's what we've seen through history. Nothing is permanent.

core_ideas.explanation: Average height mostly reflects childhood nutrition and illness rather than genetics. Ajay notes that people of Indian descent raised in advanced economies reach the same average height as people there. Each childhood illness interrupts the use of growth hormone for a while. That is why a quiz map of 19-year-old men's heights puts India near the bottom.
core_ideas.quote: Almost nothing from genetics because there are plenty papers where you take people with Indian DNA living in an advanced economy and they have the exact same average height

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay on mistranslation in a world without maps: 'There will be all kinds of confusion when Tulu is translated into Persian... The person says, I want to find a good place to get water for my horses. And the person thinks the question was, Where can the horses ford the river?'
Ajay recalls a traveller's account that Shah Jahan was 'more or less convinced that most of the world is ruled by him.' Amit: 'That's the main character syndrome in a geographical sense.'
Ajay on the ban on selling border-area maps: 'All the survey of India maps are there in the museum in London. So any self-respecting terrorist will go to London and get those maps.'
Amit's pun: 'And since we all stand on the shoulders of giants, it could well be said that Indian map makers since Everest have climbed Mount Everest.'
Amit: 'if Uber was using Survey of India data, if they had access to it, you know, you and I would be traveling by train. So you know thank God for that.'
Ajay on the joys of Google Earth: 'You can be rotating around Nanda Devi, visualizing where the plutonium might be hiding.'

Following up last week's 'stories that should be films' episode, Amit pitches a new film: two OSM volunteers meet at a mapping meetup and go map-making together. Things go wrong, but they come back together in the end, because what is the movie called? 'It's called Awesome. I just told you.'

Ajay imagines his pre-satellite self: 'I would be this old guy with white hair pontificating that the journey to economic development generally takes about 100 years. So we can hope that in 2125 India will have a good quality survey of India.'
Ajay: 'Our equipment is better than Satyajit Ray. It is our imaginations that are the constraint.' Amit agrees about the equipment, then adds: 'You know, no one is better than Satyajit Ray.'
When Amit announces a quiz, Ajay squeals: 'An exam. An exam. I love exams.' Amit: 'I have rarely seen you so excited.' Ajay: 'Even if I get zero on five.'

Amit's map quiz: Ajay recognises Tolkien's Middle-earth at once ('the land of Mordor where the shadows lie'). He mistakes George Orwell's 1984 map of Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia for a map of malaria or yellow fever. He guesses fertility rate for a map of linguistic diversity, on which India leads the world, even after Amit gives the clue by speaking three languages. The last two maps show how mothers are treated (India does badly) and the heights of 19-year-old men.

Amit, after Ajay mentions walking to the India-China border: 'I walk to the edge of the Pakistan Afghanistan border, don't ask me how... where people aren't allowed to go but I managed. But that's a story for another day.'
Amit on the possibly apocryphal Saudi censorship of a road movie with every shot of women driving removed: 'therefore Thelma and Louise in Saudi Arabia was four minutes.'
Ajay defining a true public good: 'you cannot even theoretically exclude a newborn child from the glories of Linux.'
Amit opens by promising 'instructions for dancing,' a phrase from the Magnetic Fields lyric 'It's full of charts and facts and figures and instructions for dancing,' which he reads out later.

Robert Clive and the Battle of Plassey: Ajay dates British map-making in India to 1767, 'a scant ten years after the Battle of Plassey,' starting in the parts of Bengal and Bihar the British controlled.

George Everest's great survey covered British India with interlocking triangles, about 30 km a side as Ajay recalls. Along the way it found that the peak now called Mount Everest was the highest point in India, and the work led to the Survey of India.
Novelist E.L. Doctorow's line, quoted by Amit as advice for writers: 'If you can see the light from your headlights, you can make the whole distance that way.'
